chunks: Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, who said:

I performed the Sa'i between As-Safa and Al-Marwah, along with 'Ubaydullah ibn Rashid. I said to him, 'Keep count for me.' So he began counting, considering a trip forth and back as one Shawt. When we reached a similar count, I asked him, 'How do you count?' He said, 'A trip forth and back is one Shawt.' So we completed fourteen Shawt. We mentioned this to Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), and he said, 'They have added to what is incumbent upon them; there is no penalty upon them.'

And whoever forgets and performs eight Shawt, then becomes certain, let him add six more; if he wishes, he may stop, and if he wishes, he may cut it short by discarding one, according to what we have previously narrated.

key_terms.أَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Abu 'Abdillah (Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, peace be upon him)
key_terms.الصَّفَا: As-Safa (the hill from which Sa'i begins)
key_terms.شَوْطاً: Shawt (a single round/trip between Safa and Marwah)
key_terms.لَيْسَ عَلَيْهِمْ شَيْءٌ: There is no penalty/obligation upon them
key_terms.وَالْمَرْوَةِ: Al-Marwah (the hill to which Sa'i proceeds)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if one forgets the number of rounds in Sa'i and is unsure whether they performed seven or eight?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the juristic status of Sa'i by distinguishing between the obligatory seven rounds and the recommended practice of performing fourteen, as evidenced by the companions' count. It further provides a practical legal solution for doubt (shakk), allowing those uncertain between seven and eight rounds to either complete the count to eight or stop at seven, reflecting the Shia principle of ease in ritual obligations. This ruling underscores the flexibility within the fiqh of Hajj, prioritizing certainty over rigid adherence when memory fails.
